images.title: Steel mills along the river in Pittsburgh in the 1890s
images.description: Pittsburgh's steel district in the 1890s, when America passed Britain as the world's leading industrial nation.

images.title: A water-powered textile mill in the mid-1800s
images.description: Before the Civil War most American factories still ran on water power, the system coal and steam would soon replace.

images.title: A Union Pacific railroad depot
images.description: A Union Pacific depot: the railroads that started the industrial loop.

images.title: Workers laying steel rails on a railroad in the late 1800s
images.description: Steel rails that actually lasted: every mile of track made the next mile cheaper, feeding the railroad-steel loop.

images.title: Portrait of Henry Bessemer
images.description: Englishman Henry Bessemer, who patented his steelmaking process in 1856, making steel cheap for the first time.

images.title: A preserved Bessemer converter on display in Pittsburgh
images.description: A Bessemer converter preserved on Pittsburgh's Monongahela riverfront: the vessel that blasted air through molten iron to make cheap steel after 1856.

images.title: The Corliss steam engine at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition
images.description: The giant Corliss engine at the 1876 Centennial: the machines-making-machines loop of the Second Industrial Revolution.

images.title: The Drake well at Titusville, Pennsylvania, 1859
images.description: Edwin Drake's 1859 well at Titusville, the first commercial oil well; oil went from lamp fuel to the lubricant of every machine in America.

images.title: Portrait of Thomas Edison
images.description: Edison, whose sellable system, the bulb plus the power plants to feed it, electrified American industry.

images.title: Edison's laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey
images.description: Edison's Menlo Park workshop, set up in 1876, where the practical light bulb followed in 1879.

images.title: An early Edison incandescent light bulb
images.description: The 1879 bulb: Edison's real move was the whole system, bulb plus power plants, not the invention of electricity.

images.title: Dynamos in an early electric power station
images.description: Power plants to feed the bulbs: the electrical system that let factories ditch water power for good.

images.title: Anthracite coal miners in Pennsylvania
images.description: Anthracite miners in Pennsylvania: the hard coal that let factories ditch water power for steam.

images.title: Map of the United States railroad network around 1890
images.description: The national market: one factory could suddenly sell to the whole country by rail.

images.title: A railroad construction crew laying track
images.description: A railroad crew laying track: the railroad boom that fed the steel boom.

images.title: Workers inside a Bessemer steel plant in the 1880s
images.description: The railroads' hunger for rails made cheap steel worth inventing; cheap steel then supercharged everything else.

images.title: The U.S. Capitol at Washington
images.description: Washington mostly stood back from the economy: laissez-faire, plus railroad land grants and tariffs shielding American goods.

images.title: A map of federal land grants to railroads
images.description: Federal land grants to the railroads: Washington's biggest giveaway to private industry.

images.title: The Homestead Steel Works
images.description: Carnegie's Homestead Steel Works, serving a national market: the vehicle for vertical integration.

images.title: Portrait of John D. Rockefeller
images.description: Rockefeller, the mirror image of Carnegie: horizontal integration, buying up rival refineries.

images.title: A cartoon of Standard Oil as an octopus
images.description: Standard Oil as an octopus with a tentacle around every rival: Rockefeller bought the refineries one after another until his was the only game that mattered.

images.title: A Standard Oil trust certificate from the 1880s
images.description: The trust: stockholders handed control of their shares to one board. The first and most famous: Standard Oil, 1882.

images.title: Portrait of Senator John Sherman of Ohio
images.description: Sherman's name went on the 1890 Antitrust Act that outlawed the trusts, on paper.

images.title: Standard Oil refineries at Cleveland, Ohio
images.description: The prediction beat: with trusts outlawed in 1890, Rockefeller's move was the holding company.

images.title: Inside the Standard Oil Building at 26 Broadway, New York
images.description: Inside Standard Oil's headquarters at 26 Broadway: the holding company that replaced the trust.

images.title: The United States Supreme Court in the 1890s
images.description: In 1895 the Court ruled manufacturing wasn't interstate commerce, so the Sherman Act couldn't touch most trusts.

images.title: The Capitol dome in the 1890s
images.description: The trap: the Sherman Act did not break up Standard Oil. The trusts kept running; the lawyers changed the paperwork.

images.title: Wooden oil barrels awaiting shipment in the 1890s
images.description: The Act banned trusts on paper; Standard Oil reorganized and kept refining some ninety percent of America's oil.

images.title: Workers inside a watch factory
images.description: Factory workers on the line: the new industrial workforce, often women and immigrants.

images.title: A young Andrew Carnegie
images.description: Carnegie came to America as a poor Scottish kid and climbed from the bottom of the railroad business to owning steel.

images.title: A railroad telegraph office in the 1860s
images.description: Carnegie started at the bottom of the railroad business before he ever touched steel.

images.title: John D. Rockefeller, painted in 1917
images.description: John D. Rockefeller, painted in 1917: the horizontal integrator of the oil industry.

images.title: An oil well near Pithole, Pennsylvania, in 1865
images.description: A Pennsylvania oil well in 1865: the oil country Rockefeller's companies came to dominate.

images.title: Pithole, Pennsylvania, in 1895
images.description: Pithole, an oil boom town: Rockefeller squeezed rivals through price wars and pooling agreements until his companies refined most of America's oil.

images.title: A rolling mill in the 1890s
images.description: A rolling mill: where steel became rails, beams, and wire.

images.title: Blast furnace cooling pipes at a steel works
images.description: Cooling pipes on a blast furnace: the relentless cost-cutting machinery of vertical integration.

images.title: A Carnegie public library building
images.description: Carnegie's Gospel of Wealth in brick: libraries funded by the steel fortune, free to the public.

images.title: Carnegie Hall in New York in the 1890s
images.description: Carnegie Hall, opened 1891: more of Carnegie's money, given back as the Gospel of Wealth preached.

images.title: The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh
images.description: The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh: the Gospel of Wealth in stone, libraries and universities funded by a steel fortune.

images.title: An 1892 political cartoon of Andrew Carnegie sitting on bags of money
images.description: Promise and Performance: an 1892 cartoon drawing Carnegie atop bags of money during the Homestead strike, the saint-and-sinner debate in one image.

images.title: Steelworkers during the Homestead strike of 1892
images.description: The criticism: Carnegie could only afford the giving because of the taking, crushing workers at Homestead in 1892.

images.title: The confrontation at Homestead in July 1892
images.description: The prosecution's case: Carnegie Steel's own men at Homestead in 1892, met with private armies and the state militia.

images.title: Portrait of Herbert Spencer
images.description: English philosopher Herbert Spencer, whose survival of the fittest was cooked into Social Darwinism.

images.title: Mansions along Fifth Avenue in the 1890s
images.description: Their mansions lined Fifth Avenue while workers' families lived in tenements with no windows.

images.title: A New York tenement interior photographed by Jacob Riis
images.description: The tenements a few avenues east of the mansions: the other half of the Gilded Age.

images.title: The Brooklyn Bridge in the 1880s
images.description: The defense: without Carnegie, steel stays expensive and the modern city never gets built.

images.title: The Flatiron Building under construction in 1902
images.description: A steel-framed skyscraper rising in 1902: without cheap Carnegie steel, the modern city never gets built.

images.title: Steelworkers tending a converter in the 1890s
images.description: The men who made the steel worked brutal shifts for pennies, and asking for more brought private armies.

images.title: An American industrial city around 1900
images.description: The methods were brutal, and the results transformed the economy: the country got richer with them.

images.title: Carnegie's Edgar Thomson Steel Works
images.description: The synthesis: the same mills made steel cheap and squeezed workers. The evidence cuts both ways.

images.title: Andrew Carnegie
images.description: Andrew Carnegie: captain of industry to his admirers, robber baron to his critics. The exam wants both.

images.title: John D. Rockefeller photographed in the 1890s
images.description: Both: the wealth built the modern economy, and the methods concentrated power while crushing competitors.

images.title: An American steam locomotive of the 1880s
images.description: Recap one: the engine, railroads, cheap Bessemer steel, oil, electricity, and a government that mostly got out of the way.

images.title: Oil City, Pennsylvania, in 1870
images.description: Oil City in 1870: the Pennsylvania oil country consolidated, rival by rival, into Standard Oil.

images.title: The reading room of the Carnegie Library of Atlanta
images.description: Inside a Carnegie library: the Gospel of Wealth in brick and tile, reading rooms funded by the steel fortune.

images.title: A steelworker at the Homestead Works
images.description: A steelworker dwarfed by the machinery at Homestead: the libraries were paid for with the money that squeezed the workers.

images.title: Street children in New York photographed by Jacob Riis
images.description: Recap four: the verdict. Captains built the modern economy; robbers concentrated the power and crushed the workers.

images.title: An engraving of the Bessemer steelmaking process
images.description: Question one: without Bessemer's process, steel stays too expensive for rails, bridges, or skyscrapers.

images.title: Rolling steel rails in a 19th-century mill
images.description: The stronger answer is Bessemer's process: you can't vertically integrate a product that doesn't exist yet.

images.title: A Puck magazine cover from January 1892
images.description: Puck, the Gilded Age satirical press, in 1892: cartoonists drew millionaires like Carnegie as half saint, half sinner.

images.title: Troops arriving during the Homestead Strike
images.description: State militia arriving at Homestead in 1892: the strike that exposed the taking behind the giving.

images.title: A cartoon of Uncle Sam attacking the Coal Trust
images.description: Uncle Sam axes the Coal Trust's roots: the trust-busting spirit behind the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890.

images.title: The Supreme Court chamber in the Capitol
images.description: The courts gutted the Act: in 1895 the Court ruled manufacturing wasn't interstate commerce.

images.title: The preserved Bethlehem Steel works
images.description: The preserved Bethlehem Steel works: the kind of integrated mill Carnegie's vertical empire pioneered.

images.title: John D. Rockefeller
images.description: Vertical. Horizontal. Carnegie's. The answers that keep the names straight.

images.title: Steel furnaces glowing at night in Pittsburgh
images.description: Steel built the century, and the bill came due: next, labor versus capital.
